title: Monkeys send 40 people to the hospital in Nepal as they raid homes and shops - Yahoo
description: Monkeys send 40 people to the hospital in Nepal as they raid homes and shops  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
In Nepalgunj, Nepal, monkey attacks are disrupting everyday life and sending residents to the hospital.

Reports from the city describe monkeys getting into houses and businesses to attack people, and officials are now trying to figure out how to better protect residents.

Here's what to know

According to Nepal News, dozens of residents in Nepalgunj have sought medical care after encounters with monkeys as the incidents have spread across neighborhoods and businesses. In the past month and a half alone, Bheri Hospital has treated 40 people for monkey bites.

Repeated accounts of monkeys entering homes and stores have rattled the area. Families and workers say the attacks are interrupting routine life in places where they would ordinarily expect to feel safe.

Nepal News also heard from local Pravez Khan, who said monkeys entered his house and attacked three relatives. Dr. Badri Chapagain described the rise in these attacks as a "concerning" trend.

More background

The incidents in Nepalgunj are part of a broader pattern of tension between people and wildlife, even though monkey attacks on humans remain relatively uncommon. Climate change can intensify those conflicts by increasing competition for food and space and pushing animals into new areas.

Flooding in Nepal, including August flash floods and another major river flood, swept away homes and bridges and damaged part of a hydropower station. When extreme weather upends human communities and animal habitats at the same time, dangerous encounters can become more frequent.

What's being done?

Authorities are working on protections for residents, though they have not yet spelled out what those measures will be.

According to the CDC, bites or scratches that break the skin carry higher risk, and wounds to the head, torso, and neck are even riskier.

title: Nepal resumes power exports to Bangladesh after flood disruption - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal resumes power exports to Bangladesh after flood disruption  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal resumed exporting 40 megawatts of electricity to Bangladesh through India’s transmission network on Friday evening, after the August 26 Bhotekoshi flood damage to two hydropower plants disrupted supplies.

The exports had been suspended after the disaster damaged the Trishuli and Chilime hydropower plants, both of which had been approved to supply electricity to Bangladesh. The flood damage also partially affected electricity exports to Haryana under bilateral power sales agreements.

Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) Managing Director Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha said exports resumed after India’s Central Electricity Authority approved electricity generated by other hydropower plants for supply to Bangladesh.

Under the revised arrangement, electricity from the Solu Khola and Kabeli B1 hydropower plants has been approved for export to Bangladesh, while the Lower Modi Khola plant has been cleared to supply Haryana. The new approvals replace the previous designations for the Trishuli, Chilime and Devighat hydropower plants.

Shrestha said the resumption of exports to Bangladesh, alongside continued electricity sales from other projects despite flood damage to hydropower plants and transmission infrastructure, was an important development for Nepal’s electricity trade. The renewed exports are expected to help Nepal manage surplus electricity generated during the monsoon and expand regional power trade, he said.

The NEA and the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) signed a five-year agreement on October 3, 2024, for seasonal electricity exports. Under the agreement, Nepal supplies 40 megawatts of electricity to Bangladesh each year from June 15 to November 15.

Meanwhile, the NEA exported electricity worth Rs5.925 billion to India between mid-September and mid-October 2026, earning more than in the same period last year and the preceding month despite flood damage to several hydropower projects.

According to data from the NEA’s Load Dispatch Centre, Nepal exported 633.986 million units of electricity to India during the period, generating Rs5.925 billion in revenue. Floods had forced some hydropower plants that had received approval to supply electricity to India to shut down, affecting exports.

Export earnings were Rs962 million higher than the Rs4.963 billion recorded during the same period last year and Rs832.5 million above the Rs5.0925 billion earned between mid-August and mid-September this year.

The electricity was sold through two channels. Under bilateral power sales agreements, Nepal supplied electricity to the Indian states of Haryana and Bihar. The remaining power was sold at competitive rates through the day-ahead and real-time markets of the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX).

The NEA exports surplus electricity generated during the monsoon after meeting domestic demand. Under medium-term bilateral power sales agreements, Nepal supplies electricity to Haryana and Bihar from June to October each year.

During the first three months of the current fiscal year 2026-27, Nepal exported electricity worth a total of Rs16.1513 billion.

title: UML questions Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle’s remarks on Nepali nationalism in India - OnlineKhabar English News
description: UML questions Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle’s remarks on Nepali nationalism in India  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle

Kathmandu, October 25

The CPN-UML has questioned Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle’s statement that the era of linking Nepali nationalism with anti-Indian sentiment has ended.

Niraj Acharya, head of the UML’s Publicity Department, questioned the political message and diplomatic rationale behind Wagle’s remarks during his visit to New Delhi, India.

In a social media post, Acharya said Nepal is a sovereign nation with an independent foreign policy based on sovereign equality, mutual respect and national interest.

Nepal has been a member of the United Nations since 1955, he noted, adding that Wagle was unlikely to be unaware of these fundamental principles.

“The political message and diplomatic justification for declaring during a visit to India that the old narrative linking Nepali nationalism with anti-Indian sentiment has ended are open to question,” Acharya wrote. “Nepali nationalism is not based solely on opposition to India.”

He said protecting national independence, sovereignty and national interests was an integral part of nationalism. Strengthening relations with India, he added, should not come at the expense of Nepal’s national interests and dignity.

Wagle is currently visiting India. Speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi, he said the era of associating Nepali nationalism with anti-Indianism had come to an end.

He said the aspirations of the younger generation centred on economic prosperity and good governance, adding that Nepal’s foreign policy was moving in a positive direction.

According to Wagle, decades of ideological conditioning had helped establish a narrative that equated Nepali nationalism with opposition to India.

“But our generation is different. We have seen the world, and our aspirations are economic. We want good jobs, good governance and good relations with our neighbours,” Wagle said. “So I can say with great happiness that the era of linking Nepali nationalism with anti-Indianism is now over.”

Acharya said Nepal-India relations were rooted in historical, geographical, economic, social and cultural ties, with cooperation and dialogue continuing since the establishment of formal diplomatic relations.

He said the relationship should continue to develop on the basis of mutual respect, trust, equality and shared interests.

“Maintaining friendly relations with neighbours is a necessity for Nepal, but that does not require us to refrain from expressing our national concerns and perspectives, or to engage in excessive flattery,” Acharya wrote.

Arguing that diplomacy was not simply about criticising or praising another country, he said Nepal should protect its national interests while expanding cooperation in areas of mutual benefit.

He identified trade, transit, energy, investment and connectivity as key areas for cooperation with India, while stressing that Nepal must also clearly present its position on bilateral concerns, including border disputes.

“Both the idea that disagreeing with a friendly country will damage relations and the notion that all disagreements should be set aside in the name of improving ties, effectively adopting an attitude of total submission, are extreme positions,” Acharya said.

He added that a country pursuing an independent foreign policy must express its views according to its own national interests and priorities.

“Questions naturally arise about the message conveyed when, while visiting another country, a leader characterises their own country’s nationalist perspective as outdated or irrelevant,” he wrote.

Acharya said Nepal-India relations were neither built solely through temporary political statements nor determined by the views of any single leader.

“This is a relationship connected to the people of both countries, their shared history and their long-term interests,” he said, adding that Nepal’s interests would be best served by diplomacy based on mutual respect, clear national positions and practical cooperation, free from both unnecessary flattery and provocation.

An earthquake with a magnitude of 4.2 struck the Baitadi district in Nepal on Sunday afternoon. The epicenter was located in the Dilasaini area near the Nepal-India border. Residents in surrounding areas of Baitadi and Darchula experienced the tremor as well. There are no reports of physical damage or casualties resulting from this earthquake. Nepal is prone to earthquakes due to its location in an active tectonic zone.

Nepal has been provisionally allocated $21.6 million from the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) following the devastating floods of August 2026, marking the first time the climate fund has earmarked assistance for a specific disaster. However, the amount falls short of the Himalayan nation’s estimated $4.77 billion reconstruction requirements.

The decision was taken during an extraordinary meeting of the fund’s board this week, following sustained pressure for emergency assistance. Nepal submitted its funding proposal on August 31, after seeking support through a letter to the FRLD in August, less than a week after the disaster.

According to a Reuters report published on October 23, Nepal’s government had announced that it would receive $20 million in assistance.

The August 26 disaster along the Bhote Koshi River was triggered by a chain of events involving a massive rock-and-ice avalanche and partial glacier collapse on Langtang Lirung mountain, near the Nepal-China border. Warming temperatures and geological changes in the mountain region have been linked to the catastrophe.

According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, at least 1,451 people died and 5,745 remained missing. Reuters reported that approximately 1,500 people were killed, with more than 5,000 still unaccounted for. Official figures indicated that the floods affected around 60,000 people belonging to 15,000 families.

The torrents swept away settlements and damaged critical infrastructure, including roads, bridges, schools and 13 hydropower plants. Several hydropower dams in the Trishuli river system were also destroyed. Nepal’s government estimated the losses and damage at approximately $2.7 billion, while a joint post-disaster needs assessment by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and the National Planning Commission placed recovery costs at $4.77 billion, according to Nepal News.

The assistance therefore represents less than 0.5% of the estimated reconstruction bill, highlighting the gap between available international climate finance and the needs of disaster-hit countries.

Established at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, in 2022, the FRLD was operationalised at COP28 in Dubai in 2023. Its mandate is to support developing countries particularly vulnerable to climate change. The fund’s initial operational phase, known as the Barbados Implementation Modalities (BIM), was introduced after its first call for proposals was announced at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025.

FRLD Executive Director Ibrahima Cheikh Diong said the decision demonstrated the fund’s ability to respond to urgent requirements. “By stepping up to meet this moment, the Board has shown that we can adapt our operations to the pressing needs on the ground,” he said. He added that it marked progress towards fulfilling the fund’s mandate.

Climate campaigners, however, have called for a permanent emergency response mechanism and increased contributions from developed countries, which have historically contributed disproportionately to global emissions.

Harjeet Singh, global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, has been quoted by The Times of India to say that the allocation marked a historic first step but should not remain a one-off response. He called for a permanent rapid-response mechanism that could deliver assistance within days rather than months, criticising the seven-week wait to convene the fund’s first emergency meeting.

Singh said developed countries backed the Nepal allocation while maintaining that it should neither establish a precedent nor determine the fund’s long-term operating model.

Refugees International’s senior advocate and Climate Displacement Program manager, Jocelyn Perry, called for simplified direct funding access for community organisations, including informal groups and unregistered collectives, to enable locally driven recovery.

The Fill the Fund campaign cited estimates that economic losses and damage in developing countries could average around $400 billion annually by 2030, warning that allocations worth tens of millions of dollars for individual disasters remain far below the scale of the challenge.

In September, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, used his maiden address to the United Nations to describe the disaster as a global warning and blamed climate change for the floods, despite Nepal’s negligible emissions.

Nepal has decided to issue letters of intent to private companies seeking to enter cross-border electricity trading, according to a report by news agency Press Trust of India. However, the companies will have to wait for amendments to the country's Electricity Act and obtain licences before they can begin trading.

The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation took the decision on Friday. Twelve companies, including Nepal Power Exchange, NIFRA Trading and Energy Exchange, Green Energy Power Trading and Trans Asia Power Trading, have applied for letters of intent, The Kathmandu Post reported on Saturday.

The Nepal Electricity Authority is currently the country's designated agency for cross-border electricity trade with India. Nepal also exports hydropower to Bangladesh through India's transmission network.

title: NNMGA warns of heavy Himalayan snowfall on Oct 29-30 as Bay of Bengal system heads toward Nepal - The Tourism Times
description: NNMGA warns of heavy Himalayan snowfall on Oct 29-30 as Bay of Bengal system heads toward Nepal  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) has issued a weather alert, warning that a system developing over the Bay of Bengal could bring heavy weather to Nepal on October 29 and 30, with heavy snowfall in the Himalayas above the freezing level.

The alert, prepared with senior meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, is based on the GFS forecast model, which it describes as indicative. According to the note, a system that began developing over the east-central Bay of Bengal on October 24 is expected to become a depression on October 25 and a deep depression on October 26, moving westward.

On October 27 it may intensify into a cyclone over the west-central Bay of Bengal, near coastal Andhra Pradesh. The NNMGA said it is too early to say whether the system will move inland, but that it is likely to cross coastal Andhra Pradesh and southern Odisha on October 28 and then move north-northwest or north.

On October 28, thin high clouds may spread over Nepal, especially above 6,500-7,000m, with occasional 1-2cm of snow over the eastern Himalayas, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. On October 29-30, the remnants of the system are expected to move toward the Gangetic plains and adjoining Nepal, bringing "significantly heavy" weather activity, the note said.

For October 31, the NNMGA said it was too early to forecast, but clouds may remain into the morning, or some snow may fall in the Himalayas.
